statement.text:
Two Problems in Mechanics
Part A: a wooden cylinder of radius \(r_1\), thickness \(h_1\), density \(\rho_1\), and total mass \(M\) contains a metal disk replacing wood. Its density is \(\rho_2>\rho_1\), radius \(r_2\), thickness \(h_2\), and axis B is parallel to cylinder axis S at distance \(d\). The disk is midway between the end faces. Known quantities are \(r_1,h_1,\rho_1,\rho_2,M\). Let the centre of mass C be distance \(b\) from S. Part B: a wheel-shaped space station of radius \(R\) rotates at angular speed \(\omega_{ss}\). Astronauts live on the inside rim. Ignore the station gravity and local floor curvature where specified. Earth has radius \(R_E\) and surface gravity \(g_E\).
A.1. Centre of mass offset


On a horizontal surface the cylinder is in stable equilibrium. Slowly incline the surface through \(\Theta\). The cylinder rolls without slipping and reaches equilibrium after rotating through the measured angle \(\phi\) shown. Determine \(b\).
A.2. Suspended-cylinder period

Suspend the cylinder at S, displace it through a small angle \(\varphi\), and measure period \(T\). Find the equation of motion and inertia \(I_S\).
A.3. Disk offset
Express \(d\) in terms of \(b\) and known quantities, allowing \(r_2,h_2\).
A.4. Geometrical inertia
Find \(I_S\) from geometry using \(b\), the known quantities, and optionally \(r_2,h_2\).
A.5. Hidden-disk dimensions
Determine \(r_2,h_2\) in terms of the measured \(b,T\) and known quantities.
B.1. Artificial gravity

Find the rotation rate producing gravity \(g_E\) at the rim.
B.2. Earth spring oscillator
A mass \(m\) on a spring of stiffness \(k\) moves only vertically. Find its angular frequency in uniform terrestrial gravity.
B.3. Station spring oscillator
Find the angular oscillation frequency when horizontal motion is constrained in the station.
B.4. Terrestrial gravity gradient
Include the first-order height dependence of Earth gravity. Find \(g_E(h)\) and angular oscillator frequency \(\widetilde\omega_E\). Ignore Earth rotation.
B.5. Indistinguishable frequencies
For which station radius do B.3 and B.4 coincide?
B.6. Small-height drop
Drop a mass from height \(H\ll R\). Assuming constant downward acceleration and \(d_x\ll H\), find horizontal velocity and displacement at the floor. Either consistent horizontal sign convention is allowed.
B.7. Return to the tower base
A sufficiently tall tower allows the released mass to hit its base, with zero relative horizontal displacement. Find the smallest nonzero height for this to occur.
B.8. Unconstrained oscillator trajectory

The spring hangs from a ring free to slide horizontally. Let y point towards the station centre and pull the mass to \(x=0,y=-d\), then release at rest. Neglect Coriolis feedback on vertical motion. Find \(x(t),y(t)\), and sketch the trajectory, marking amplitudes and cusps.

children.text: The centre of mass lies vertically above the contact point, so the common horizontal offset satisfies \(b\sin\phi=r_1\sin\Theta\). Hence \[b=r_1\sin\Theta/\sin\phi.\]
Define excess disk mass \(\Delta M=\pi r_2^2h_2(\rho_2-\rho_1)=M-\pi r_1^2h_1\rho_1\). The uniform wood contribution has centre S, so \(Mb=\Delta M d\) and \(d=Mb/\Delta M\).
The parallel-axis theorem gives \[I_S=\tfrac12\pi h_1\rho_1r_1^4+\tfrac12\Delta M r_2^2+\frac{M^2b^2}{\Delta M}.\] Here \(\Delta M=M-\pi r_1^2h_1\rho_1\).

Use \(I_S=MgbT^2/(4\pi^2)\) and the previous inertia: \[r_2=\sqrt{\frac2{\Delta M}\left[\frac{MgbT^2}{4\pi^2}-\frac{\pi h_1\rho_1r_1^4}{2}-\frac{M^2b^2}{\Delta M}\right]},\qquad h_2=\frac{\Delta M}{\pi r_2^2(\rho_2-\rho_1)}.\] These require a physically admissible positive radicand and a disk fitting inside the wood.
Gravity shifts equilibrium without changing stiffness. Thus \(\omega_E=\sqrt{k/m}\).
The centrifugal force varies linearly with radius. After shifting equilibrium, \(m\ddot y+(k-m\omega_{ss}^2)y=0\). Hence \(\omega=\sqrt{k/m-\omega_{ss}^2}\), assuming positive effective stiffness.
The downward magnitude is \(g_E(h)=g_E(1+h/R_E)^{-2}\simeq g_E(1-2h/R_E)\). The upward variation reduces restoring stiffness, so \[\widetilde\omega_E=\sqrt{k/m-2g_E/R_E}.\]

The fall time is \(t_f=\sqrt{2H/(\omega_{ss}^2R)}\). Integrate the Coriolis acceleration magnitude \(2\omega_{ss}g_Et\): \[|v_x|=2H\omega_{ss},\qquad |d_x|=\frac13\sqrt{\frac{8H^3}{R}}.\] Relative to the rotating floor the mass falls behind the tower for the usual forward-positive convention.
B.7. Return to the tower base

In the inertial frame the mass moves straight at speed \(\omega_{ss}(R-H)\). Put \(u=\omega_{ss}t_f=\sqrt{R^2-(R-H)^2}/(R-H)\). Returning to the base requires \(\tan u=u\) with the correct angular branch and \(\cos u>0\). The first admissible nonzero root is \(u=7.72525\), between \(2\pi\) and \(5\pi/2\). Thus \(H/R=1-1/\sqrt{1+u^2}=0.87162\). The root near 4.493 has negative cosine and does not describe a tower inside the rim.

Write \(\omega=\sqrt{k/m-\omega_{ss}^2}\). Then \(y=-d\cos\omega t\). Choosing \(\ddot x=-2\omega_{ss}\dot y\), integrate twice with zero initial velocity: \[x=\frac{2\omega_{ss}d}{\omega}\sin\omega t-2\omega_{ss}dt.\] The opposite horizontal sign is equivalent. The path has vertical extrema \(\pm d\), a drift, and cusps at \(y=-d\), separated horizontally by \(4\pi\omega_{ss}d/\omega\). The source prints an inconsistent sign for \(\dot y\). Differentiating the stated \(y(t)\) and using a single Coriolis convention resolves it.

solution.text:
Two Problems in Mechanics
A.1. Centre of mass offset
The centre of mass lies vertically above the contact point, so the common horizontal offset satisfies \(b\sin\phi=r_1\sin\Theta\). Hence \[b=r_1\sin\Theta/\sin\phi.\]
A.2. Suspended-cylinder period
The torque is \(-Mgb\sin\varphi\), so \(I_S\ddot\varphi=-Mgb\sin\varphi\simeq-Mgb\varphi\). Thus \[I_S=MgbT^2/(4\pi^2).\]
A.3. Disk offset
Define excess disk mass \(\Delta M=\pi r_2^2h_2(\rho_2-\rho_1)=M-\pi r_1^2h_1\rho_1\). The uniform wood contribution has centre S, so \(Mb=\Delta M d\) and \(d=Mb/\Delta M\).
A.4. Geometrical inertia
The parallel-axis theorem gives \[I_S=\tfrac12\pi h_1\rho_1r_1^4+\tfrac12\Delta M r_2^2+\frac{M^2b^2}{\Delta M}.\] Here \(\Delta M=M-\pi r_1^2h_1\rho_1\).
A.5. Hidden-disk dimensions
Use \(I_S=MgbT^2/(4\pi^2)\) and the previous inertia: \[r_2=\sqrt{\frac2{\Delta M}\left[\frac{MgbT^2}{4\pi^2}-\frac{\pi h_1\rho_1r_1^4}{2}-\frac{M^2b^2}{\Delta M}\right]},\qquad h_2=\frac{\Delta M}{\pi r_2^2(\rho_2-\rho_1)}.\] These require a physically admissible positive radicand and a disk fitting inside the wood.
B.1. Artificial gravity
Equate \(\omega_{ss}^2R=g_E\), giving \(\omega_{ss}=\sqrt{g_E/R}\).
B.2. Earth spring oscillator
Gravity shifts equilibrium without changing stiffness. Thus \(\omega_E=\sqrt{k/m}\).
B.3. Station spring oscillator
The centrifugal force varies linearly with radius. After shifting equilibrium, \(m\ddot y+(k-m\omega_{ss}^2)y=0\). Hence \(\omega=\sqrt{k/m-\omega_{ss}^2}\), assuming positive effective stiffness.
B.4. Terrestrial gravity gradient
The downward magnitude is \(g_E(h)=g_E(1+h/R_E)^{-2}\simeq g_E(1-2h/R_E)\). The upward variation reduces restoring stiffness, so \[\widetilde\omega_E=\sqrt{k/m-2g_E/R_E}.\]
B.5. Indistinguishable frequencies
Equate \(g_E/R=2g_E/R_E\), giving \(R=R_E/2\).
B.6. Small-height drop
The fall time is \(t_f=\sqrt{2H/(\omega_{ss}^2R)}\). Integrate the Coriolis acceleration magnitude \(2\omega_{ss}g_Et\): \[|v_x|=2H\omega_{ss},\qquad |d_x|=\frac13\sqrt{\frac{8H^3}{R}}.\] Relative to the rotating floor the mass falls behind the tower for the usual forward-positive convention.
B.7. Return to the tower base
In the inertial frame the mass moves straight at speed \(\omega_{ss}(R-H)\). Put \(u=\omega_{ss}t_f=\sqrt{R^2-(R-H)^2}/(R-H)\). Returning to the base requires \(\tan u=u\) with the correct angular branch and \(\cos u>0\). The first admissible nonzero root is \(u=7.72525\), between \(2\pi\) and \(5\pi/2\). Thus \(H/R=1-1/\sqrt{1+u^2}=0.87162\). The root near 4.493 has negative cosine and does not describe a tower inside the rim.
B.8. Unconstrained oscillator trajectory
Write \(\omega=\sqrt{k/m-\omega_{ss}^2}\). Then \(y=-d\cos\omega t\). Choosing \(\ddot x=-2\omega_{ss}\dot y\), integrate twice with zero initial velocity: \[x=\frac{2\omega_{ss}d}{\omega}\sin\omega t-2\omega_{ss}dt.\] The opposite horizontal sign is equivalent. The path has vertical extrema \(\pm d\), a drift, and cusps at \(y=-d\), separated horizontally by \(4\pi\omega_{ss}d/\omega\). The source prints an inconsistent sign for \(\dot y\). Differentiating the stated \(y(t)\) and using a single Coriolis convention resolves it.
